sentences.text: The single known specimen of this animal measures more than one meter from the skull tip to the tail base.
It was a fully terrestrial predator, living on land like other members of its family.
This creature is distinguished by unique skull features, including a nasal bone with a dorsal midline crest and a frontal ridge reaching the midline between the prefrontals.
The lower jaw shows outer sculpture limited to the dentary bone and lacks a peg on the occipital surface of the mandibular symphysis.

Aplestosuchus is distinguished from all other known crocodiliforms by a unique combination of traits, including four autapomorphies such as a crested medial supratemporal border, a lateral depression on the quadrate bone, a crested palatine bone bar, a crested coanal septum, a specific paracoanal fossa location, and a row of foramina between the mandibular fenestra and the ectopterygoid-yugal suture.
The skeleton preserves the remains of an unidentified sphagesaurid crocodyliform inside its abdominal cavity.
Baurusuchids, which could reach over four meters in length, were among the super-predators of Late Cretaceous South American ecosystems.
The fossil remains were discovered in the Buruti creek area of the General Salgado municipality in southern Brazil.
The specimen was found lying on its side, matching the death posture of other baurusuchids from the site.
Evidence suggests that the sphagesaurid material found in the abdominal cavity resulted from active predation rather than scavenging.

Aplestosuchus is classified within the family Baurusuchidae, alongside other genera like Campinasuchus and Gondwanasuchus, with non-autapomorphic traits such as the quadrate depression confirming this placement.
The animal belongs to the class Reptilia, and the type species of the genus is Aplestosuchus sordidus.
Aplestosuchus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 93.5 to 83.5 million years ago, specifically during the Campanian to Maastrichtian stages from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
